extracted.intended_audience: USPTO leadership, patent quality assurance staff, policymakers, and oversight/audit stakeholders
extracted.subtask_description: Audit-oriented guidance and standards for assessing and improving USPTO patent examination quality, including performance appraisals, OPQA independent reviews, signatory authority criteria, data collection, and controls to detect misconduct such as patent mortgaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance appraisal elements and weights
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO supervisors rate patent examiners on four performance elements: Production (35%), Quality (35%), Docket management (20%), and Stakeholder interaction (10%). Ratings use a five-point scale: outstanding, commendable, fully successful, marginal, and unacceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These elements compose the examiner's annual performance appraisal. The quality element counts for 35% of the total score and is intended to measure whether examiners correctly determine approval or rejection of patent applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality rating error-rate thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality ratings map to examiner error-rate bands (percent): Outstanding 0–4.49; Commendable 4.50–5.49; Fully Successful 5.50–6.49; Marginal 6.50–7.49; Unacceptable 7.5 or higher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An examiner's error rate (see calculation criterion) is the primary driver for the quality rating. Additional factors (indicia) may adjust ratings from outstanding to commendable, but cannot be used to assign below fully successful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supervisory review requirement (minimum four written decisions/year)
rubrics_metrics.description: Supervisors are required to conduct an in-depth review of a minimum of four written decisions per examiner each fiscal year as part of the performance appraisal process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although supervisors claim to review more, USPTO historically did not require documentation of which cases were reviewed. The minimum of four reviews versus an average examiner workload (about 73 final determinations/year) creates statistical limits on detecting poor performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of errors and counting rule for multiple errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Errors are instances in which the examiner did not comply with examining standards; they are categorized from 1 to 3 based upon severity and examiner grade level. Multiple errors in the same determination are counted as one for error-rate calculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because multiple mistakes within a single decision count as one charged error, the error rate can underrepresent the total number and severity of mistakes across determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calculation of examiner error rate
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner's error rate is defined as the number of charged errors found during the supervisor's review divided by the total number of patent determinations the examiner completed during the review period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implications: if only the four required reviews are used, errors in all four may still produce a fully successful or commendable rating given typical annual workloads (examples in report show errors in 75–100% of reviewed cases can still yield fully successful or higher).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicia used to adjust outstanding/commendable ratings
rubrics_metrics.description: Additional factors (indicia) supervisors may consider to downgrade outstanding to commendable include: clear and concise communication; early patentable determinations during prosecution; and patentable subject matter allowed early in the review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These indicia can reduce an otherwise outstanding or commendable rating, but they cannot be used to assign ratings below fully successful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Error charging, rebuttal, and coaching process
rubrics_metrics.description: When a supervisor finds an error, the examiner may rebut (orally or in writing); the supervisor can remove the error or explain why the rebuttal is unpersuasive; unresolved disagreements may be escalated to Technology Center Director and grievance per POPA agreement. Supervisors may opt to coach instead of charging an error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rebuttal process is described as time-consuming and laborious. The availability of coaching and the burden of rebuttal create incentives for supervisors to avoid charging errors—potentially understating examiner error rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: OPQA independent review scope and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office of Patent Quality Assurance (OPQA) independently reviews a statistical sample of preliminary and final examiner decisions to test for clear errors and conformance with best practices and to generate corps-wide quality measurements and training recommendations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OPQA annually reviews on average less than 1% of all office actions; OPQA's stated role is to generate statistically significant corps-wide results, not to catch every low-quality patent or to assess individual examiner performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: OPQA informal grace period after new guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: OPQA reviewers have in practice allowed a 6- to 12-month informal grace period after the issuance of new patent examination guidance before charging errors for noncompliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This was characterized as an informal practice (not approved policy) and can lead to underrepresentation of errors in the official metrics during the grace period.

rubrics_metrics.name: OPQA internal audit limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: OPQA's periodic internal audits were found to be predictable and not structured to assess unwritten or informal policies and procedures followed by some OPQA reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Predictability of audits and lack of mechanisms to detect informal practices can allow inconsistent application of error charging and categorization to persist unnoticed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signatory Authority Program eligibility and trial criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Steps and criteria for partial and full signatory authority: Partial eligibility requires GS-13 and at least 'fully successful' for 10 consecutive pay periods; temporary partial authority; trial period requiring ≥700 examining hours in 13 pay periods, ≥17 preliminary decisions reviewed by a minimum of two supervisory patent examiners, and an error rate of 6.49% or less during the period; then permanent partial authority. Full authority follows a similar process with final determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OPQA and supervisory data for signatory reviews historically were not comprehensive; USPTO did not systematically collect which decisions contained errors nor whether errors were charged during signatory determinations prior to recent periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Error severity categorization (1–3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Errors are categorized from 1 to 3 based upon severity and the examiner's grade level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The categorization affects how errors are interpreted in performance measurement and in signatory authority decisions; details of the categories (examples per category) are recorded by OPQA when documenting why a determination had an error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and limits of OPQA results in official quality metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: OPQA results feed into USPTO's official quality metrics (corps-wide accuracy rates), affect supervisor bonuses, and identify training needs, but are not used to assess individual examiners or particular USPTO offices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because OPQA samples represent less than 1% of actions and OPQA historically did not feed errors into examiner error rates for performance appraisals, OPQA-based metrics may underrepresent true error rates and do not substitute for supervisor-level case tracking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data collection requirement for supervisory and signatory reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO should collect and use available databases and systems to record information on patent applications reviewed and errors found, including supervisory reviews and Signatory Authority Program reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically supervisors were not required to systematically record when they found errors; lack of recorded data prevents analysis of trends, end-loading impacts, and proper measurement of examiner quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent mortgaging definition, detection, and disciplinary guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent mortgaging is when an employee knowingly submits incomplete work for credit (work credit abuse). USPTO treats mortgaging as misconduct and has policies identifying disciplinary factors (effect on supervisor confidence, notoriety/agency reputation, consistency with penalties imposed on others).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Between Oct 2008 and Aug 2014, 121 allegations occurred; responses varied widely from abeyance agreements to suspensions and terminations. The report recommends developing additional controls to detect and monitor mortgaging and to ensure consistent application of disciplinary policies. An abeyance agreement is commonly used (sanction agreed but not imposed provided employee meets obligations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact of FY2011 performance appraisal changes on quality measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes implemented in FY2011 included expanding OPQA assessments and revising how examiner quality was measured in annual performance assessments; some changes relaxed error thresholds by eliminating or combining multiple metrics into one quality error rate and requiring multiple occurrences before charging certain errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These changes made it more difficult to tie examiner performance to issuance of high-quality patents and likely contributed to inflation of quality ratings (higher likelihood of outstanding/commendable ratings after FY2011).

rubrics_metrics.name: Supervisor incentives and barriers affecting error charging
rubrics_metrics.description: Supervisors face disincentives to charge errors: the rebuttal process is time-consuming and charging errors can affect examiner awards/ratings; verbal guidance that OPQA-identified errors could not be used in error-rate calculations further discouraged charging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These incentives and informal directives can produce underreporting of errors in supervisory data and performance appraisals, inflating quality ratings despite identified errors.
